changes.after: Learn which uneditable fields still send a value.

before: A text field can be noneditable yet still participate in form data. readonly and disabled are different states. Earlier work established disabled omission; here compare that omission with a readonly field and a hidden value.

readonly on a supported text input prevents ordinary user editing while leaving it normally focusable and submitted when named. disabled prevents ordinary interaction and excludes this input from form data. Both are Boolean attributes. readonly does not apply to every control type, such as select or checkbox. A hidden input has no ordinary visible control but can still submit its name/value.

```html
<form id="booking">
  <label for="reference">Booking reference</label><input id="reference" name="reference" value="R17" readonly>
  <label for="estimate">Draft estimate</label><input id="estimate" name="estimate" value="12" disabled>
  <input type="hidden" name="revision" value="2">
  <button type="submit">Confirm</button>
</form>
```
The local data contains reference=R17 and revision=2, but not estimate. Constructing FormData in the supplied checker reads these pairs without contacting a server. Hidden and readonly values are not trusted secrets: a person can inspect or change page data outside normal editing, so the server must verify them independently.

Build the labeled readonly reference, labeled disabled estimate and hidden revision exactly as shown. Keep the two visible labels even though neither field is ordinarily editable. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.
after: A text input with `readonly` can be read but not edited normally. If it has a name, its value is still sent with the form. Use this when someone needs to see a value without changing it.

`disabled` does a different job. It turns off ordinary interaction with the field and leaves its value out of the form data. To turn either setting off, remove the attribute; adding the word `false` does not turn it off.

This form has three kinds of stored value.

```html
<form id="booking">
  <label for="reference">Booking reference</label><input id="reference" name="reference" value="R17" readonly>
  <label for="estimate">Draft estimate</label><input id="estimate" name="estimate" value="12" disabled>
  <input type="hidden" name="revision" value="2">
  <button type="submit">Confirm</button>
</form>
```

The readonly reference sends `reference=R17`. The disabled estimate is left out. `type="hidden"` stores `revision=2` without a visible field. Hidden values are still readable and changeable through browser tools, so they are not a safe place for secrets.

Build the shown form with id `booking`. Keep the reference labeled, named and readonly. Keep the estimate labeled, named and disabled. Add the hidden revision with value `2`. Run the checks to see which values are included. No data is sent to a service.

before.question: Replace readonly with disabled on reference. What happens to reference in ordinary form data?
choices: It is sent as an empty string.
It is omitted, although its visible value still appears in the field.
It remains submitted because its name did not change.
before.explanation: A name alone is insufficient for a disabled control to participate. readonly and disabled have different submission behavior.

after.question: You replace readonly with disabled on the reference field. What happens to its form data?
choices: It is left out, even though the value is still visible.
It is still sent because it has a name.
after.explanation: A disabled field is left out. A readonly text field can still send its named value.
